entities.name: Bagrat I of Imereti
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bagrat I "the Minor" of the Bagrationi dynasty (died 1372) was a pivotal figure in the complex fragmentation of the medieval Georgian Kingdom, specifically its western province of Imereti, during the mid-14th century. His brief reign as an independent monarch (1329-1330) and subsequent decades as a semi-autonomous duke marked a critical phase in the enduring struggle between the centralizing aspirations of the Bagratid kings of unified Georgia and the centrifugal forces of its powerful regional nobility. His actions directly contributed to the re-establishment of a distinct Imeretian polity, albeit initially as a vassalage, shaping the geopolitical landscape of the South Caucasus for centuries.

Ascending to power in 1329, Bagrat I seized the opportunity presented by the weakening grip of the unified Georgian crown, proclaiming himself King of Imereti, a title previously held by his father, Constantine I. This independent claim, however, was short-lived. In 1330, the formidable King George V "the Brilliant" of Georgia, intent on restoring the kingdom's territorial integrity and royal authority after the Mongol Yoke, launched a decisive campaign into Western Georgia. George V swiftly subdued Bagrat, forcing him to relinquish his royal title and accept the status of a *eristavi* (duke) under the Georgian crown, granting him the duchy of Chorapan, which largely corresponded to the historical Imereti.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bagrat I's actions were regionally significant for establishing a continuous ducal line in Imereti, which directly led to its re-emergence as an independent kingdom in the late 15th century, shaping the political map of medieval Georgia for centuries. His role in the temporary reunification efforts under George V also underscores the complex regional dynamics of the post-Mongol era.
